subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which structure carries air from the throat down towards the lungs?
questions.explain: The trachea (windpipe) carries air from the throat to the bronchi and lungs.

questions.q: Which muscle forms the floor of the thorax and helps with breathing?
questions.explain: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen and changes chest volume during breathing.

questions.q: Why does the trachea contain rings of cartilage?
options: To hold the airway open and stop it collapsing
To pump air into the lungs
questions.explain: The C-shaped cartilage rings support the trachea so it stays open as air is drawn in.

questions.q: What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation (breathing in)?
options: It relaxes and moves up into a dome
questions.explain: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thorax.

questions.q: During inhalation, what happens to the volume and air pressure inside the thorax?
questions.explain: The thorax volume increases so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure, and air moves in.

questions.q: What are the tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange happens called?
questions.explain: Alveoli are the microscopic air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.

questions.q: Which word equation correctly represents aerobic respiration?
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Which is the correct balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration?
questions.explain: Glucose (C6H12O6) reacts with six oxygen molecules to form six carbon dioxide and six water molecules.

questions.q: In which cell organelle does aerobic respiration mainly take place?
questions.explain: Aerobic respiration occurs in the mitochondria, where most of the cell's energy is released.

questions.q: What substance is produced when human muscle cells respire anaerobically?
questions.explain: In humans, anaerobic respiration breaks glucose down incompletely to form lactic acid.

questions.q: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
questions.explain: In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Why does aerobic respiration release more energy from glucose than anaerobic respiration?
options: The glucose is broken down completely when oxygen is present
It does not use any glucose
It produces lactic acid which stores energy
It happens in the nucleus instead
questions.explain: With oxygen the glucose is fully broken down, so far more energy is released than in incomplete anaerobic breakdown.

questions.q: After hard exercise a person breathes deeply for a while to 'repay the oxygen debt'. What is this oxygen used for?
options: To break down the lactic acid that built up in the muscles
To store glucose in the muscles
questions.explain: The extra oxygen taken in after exercise is used to break down the lactic acid produced during anaerobic respiration.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of inhaled (breathed-in) air is oxygen?
questions.explain: Inhaled air is about 21% oxygen and about 78% nitrogen, with only around 0.04% carbon dioxide.

questions.q: A student finds that their exhaled air turns limewater cloudy much faster than inhaled air. What does this show about exhaled air?
options: It contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air
It contains more oxygen than inhaled air
It contains no carbon dioxide at all
It contains more nitrogen than inhaled air
questions.explain: Exhaled air is richer in carbon dioxide (about 4%), which turns limewater cloudy more quickly.

questions.q: The wall of an alveolus is only one cell thick. How does this help gas exchange?
options: It gives a short diffusion distance for gases
It slows down the movement of gases
It stops blood reaching the alveolus
It increases the amount of nitrogen absorbed
questions.explain: Thin, one-cell-thick walls give a short diffusion path so oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged rapidly.

questions.q: Which feature of the alveoli increases the rate of gas exchange by providing more room for diffusion?
questions.explain: The huge combined surface area of the many alveoli allows a high rate of diffusion of gases.

questions.q: In the alveoli, oxygen moves from the air into the blood. By which process does this happen and in which direction?
options: Diffusion, from a high to a low oxygen concentration
Active transport, from low to high concentration
Diffusion, from a low to a high oxygen concentration
Osmosis, from the blood into the air
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from the oxygen-rich alveolar air into the oxygen-poor blood.

questions.q: A sprinter's leg muscles cannot get enough oxygen during a 100 m race. Which type of respiration are the muscles mainly using and what does it produce?
options: Aerobic respiration, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: When oxygen supply is insufficient, muscles respire anaerobically, producing lactic acid.

questions.q: When a person starts to exercise their breathing rate increases. Why is this a useful response?
options: It supplies more oxygen and removes more carbon dioxide from the body
It reduces the oxygen supply to resting muscles
It cools the lungs by adding carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Faster, deeper breathing delivers more oxygen for respiration and removes the extra carbon dioxide produced.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Biology (2017) specification; Breathing & Respiration
